english.html: mous deed, as against Sodomites, Atheists and brigands, who, being so frantic and enraged as to study nothing but inhuman and unnatural things, well deserve also to be restrained by inhumanity and ferocity of penalty <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>. But let us recover our breath a little, and the track of our path. Someone perhaps will say here that the Court was necessarily bound to condemn the said du Tilh to be burnt alive, and not after his death <sup class="mk" data-key="h">h</sup>; inasmuch as, where the law commands that some malefactor be burnt, he must be burnt fully alive <sup class="mk" data-key="i">i</sup>. Added to which, after the death of the accused all prosecution of crimes ends and is extinguished <sup class="mk" data-key="k">k</sup>, so that several have written that judges who have the dead bodies and carcasses of executed men fastened or hung upon the gibbet-forks do things unworthy of them, and err greatly <sup class="mk" data-key="l">l</sup>. To resolve which difficulty, I shall confess in the first place that to vex, torment and punish the body of a dead person, whom God has called to himself and to the judgment of his great tribunal, is a very strange thing, and one smacking of I know not what of the barbarity and inhumanity <sup class="mk" data-key="m">m</sup> with which that great name of Achilles remains still stained, when, to avenge the death of Patroclus his great friend (whom Hector son of Priam had killed), not content with having slain Hector, he had his body tied to a chariot and dragged three times around Troy and the tomb of Patroclus <sup class="mk" data-key="n">n</sup>.

english.html: Three times around the walls of Ilium he had dragged Hector (Ter circum Iliacos raptaverat Hectora muros) o.

notes.gloss: Ter circum Iliacos raptaverat Hectora muros, from the paintings in Dido's temple.

english.html: The horror and enormity of the crime may nevertheless be so great that, in detestation of it, it belongs to the example and to the greatness of a well-ordered Commonwealth to punish, roast and dismember the bodies, the carcasses, of the dead: so that the memory of persons so wretched and abominable may be wholly annihilated and lost, and that by the spectacle of such a penalty these prodigiously wicked men may be frightened and turned away from like evil deeds <sup class="mk" data-key="q">q</sup>. Thus our Accursius admonishes us to do to brigands and highway robbers, after they are hanged and strangled: namely, to expose them to famished beasts, to be torn to pieces and devoured by them <sup class="mk" data-key="r">r</sup>.
